summary:
Sol'Kanar the Tainted is a donate deck. Blink Sol'Kanar with Thassa or Conjurer's Closet to reuse its draw, drain and damage modes; give away Demonic Pact after three modes; donate Immortal Coil and exile the holder's graveyard; or push Captive Audience, Xantcha, Khârn and other liabilities onto opponents. All 4 Spellbook lines and all 14 attestation items are re-verified against the canonical list.

Rules surprises: blinking Sol'Kanar above a pending mode-4 trigger makes it fail on the new object; the earlier modes stay with the Pact no matter who controls it; a donated Pact, Coil, Archfiend or Gambit comes back to you if its holder leaves the game (CR 800.4a), while Captive Audience and Xantcha are exiled instead. One dependency-risk flag (returned liabilities) and one documentation flag (Gambit's trigger is end step, not upkeep). No list errors.

interactions.title: Sol'Kanar's "hasn't been chosen" modes belong to the object; whoever controls it makes the choices
interactions.ruling: Sol'Kanar's end-step trigger is modal, and the mode is chosen as it goes on the stack. The record of chosen modes belongs to that Sol'Kanar object. If Sol'Kanar leaves the battlefield and returns, it's a new object and all four modes are available again. A plain control change keeps the history. Once an opponent controls Sol'Kanar, it triggers in their end step and they make every choice: they draw, they drain their opponents (you included), and they pick which of their opponents gets it next.
interactions.short: Mode history is per object; a blink resets it, a control change doesn't.

oracle.quote: At the beginning of your end step, choose one that hasn't been chosen —

rulings.quote: Once Sol'kanar the Tainted is controlled by your opponent, its ability triggers during that player's end step and that player makes all choices for it. That player draws a card for its first mode and gains life for its second mode, that player's opponents lose life for its second mode, and that player chooses one of their opponents for its last mode.

interactions.title: Thassa / Conjurer's Closet: order the blink below Sol'Kanar to repeat the first three modes, or above it to dodge mode 4
interactions.ruling:
Sol'Kanar and Thassa (or Conjurer's Closet) trigger at the same time in your end step, and you choose the order.
- **Blink on the bottom:** the Sol'Kanar mode (draw, drain or 3 damage) resolves first. Then the blink returns a new object with no modes chosen, so every end step can use a first-three mode again.
- **Blink on top, when you had to choose mode 4:** Sol'Kanar is exiled and returned first. The pending trigger's "Exile Sol'Kanar" can't find the new object, so nothing is given away.

Planar Incision can also exile an opponent-controlled Sol'Kanar. It returns under its owner's control as a new object with a +1/+1 counter. Lightning Greaves is correctly out of the list, since shroud would stop your own Thassa, Closet and Incision from targeting it.
interactions.short: Blink under the trigger = repeat good modes; blink over mode 4 = it fizzles on the new object.

oracle.quote: At the beginning of your end step, exile up to one other target creature you control, then return that card to the battlefield under your control.
Exile target artifact or creature, then return it to the battlefield under its owner's control with a +1/+1 counter on it.

rulings.quote: Once the exiled creature returns, it's considered a new object with no relation to the object that it was. Auras attached to the exiled creature will be put into their owners' graveyards. Equipment attached to the exiled creature will become unattached and remain on the battlefield. Any counters on the exiled creature will cease to exist.

interactions.title: Demonic Pact donation: the recipient inherits the mode history and must take "You lose the game"
interactions.ruling: Choose Demonic Pact's first three modes yourself, then hand it over with Donate, Harmless Offering, Blim's combat trigger or a face-up Coveted Falcon. It doesn't matter who chose the earlier modes. At the recipient's next upkeep the only mode left is the fourth, so they have to choose it and lose. This is in Spellbook (2770-6676, 3090-6676, 3769-6676, 6676-6922). A Pact trigger that was countered still counts its mode as chosen.
interactions.short: Three safe modes, then give Pact away; the new controller must pick mode 4.

rulings.quote: It doesn't matter who has chosen any particular mode. For example, say you control Demonic Pact and have chosen the first two modes. If an opponent gains control of Demonic Pact, that player can choose only the third or fourth mode.
Yes, if the fourth mode is the only one remaining, you must choose it. You read the whole contract, right?
If the ability doesn't resolve (either for having its target become illegal or because a spell or ability counters it), the mode chosen for that instance of the ability still counts as being chosen.

spellbook.quote: The first three modes of Demonic Pact have been selected.
At the beginning of the opponent's upkeep, Demonic Pact triggers, causing them to select the fourth mode and lose the game.

interactions.title: Immortal Coil gift: give it away, exile their graveyard, and the state trigger can't be undone
interactions.ruling: Give Immortal Coil to an opponent. Fateful Handoff on Coil draws four (MV 4), then hands it over. Then exile their graveyard with Bojuka Bog or Rakdos Charm. Coil's "no cards in your graveyard" is a state trigger for its current controller. Once it has triggered, putting a card into the graveyard doesn't stop it. If the trigger is countered while the graveyard is still empty, it just triggers again. While they hold Coil, damage to them is prevented, so this route kills by the trigger, not by damage.
interactions.short: Donated Coil + graveyard hate = state-triggered loss that refilling the yard can't stop.

oracle.quote: When there are no cards in your graveyard, you lose the game.
Draw cards equal to the mana value of target artifact or creature you control. An opponent gains control of that permanent.

rulings.quote: The third ability checks whether your graveyard is empty only at the time it triggers. Putting a card into your graveyard after that doesn’t help. You’ll lose the game when the ability resolves.
If the third ability is countered, but your graveyard is still empty, the ability will immediately trigger again.

interactions.title: Enters-under-opponent liabilities: Captive Audience, Xantcha, Khârn
interactions.ruling:
**Captive Audience and Xantcha** enter under an opponent's control as a replacement effect, so there's no moment when you control them. The new controller makes all of Captive Audience's choices in their upkeep. Anyone, including you, can activate Xantcha's {3} ability: Xantcha's controller loses 2 and the activator draws.

**Khârn** changes controller as part of the damage-prevention replacement, in the middle of resolution. Its Sigil draw trigger waits until that resolution finishes.

**Jon Irenicus's** gift can't be sacrificed in response, because "can't be sacrificed" applies right away. Jon also draws you a card whenever a creature you own but don't control attacks.

oracle.quote: This enchantment enters under the control of an opponent of your choice.
{3}: Xantcha's controller loses 2 life and you draw a card. Any player may activate this ability.

rulings.quote: Once Captive Audience is controlled by your opponent, its ability triggers during that player’s upkeep and that player makes all choices for it. That player is affected by its first two modes, and that player’s opponents create the tokens for its last mode.

Xantcha's first ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield, not a triggered ability. Players can't take actions (such as activating its last ability) while Xantcha's on the battlefield before it's controlled by another player.

An opponent gaining control of it is part of the replacement effect and happens immediately, even if you are in the middle of resolving the spell or ability and it has more instructions to perform after taking damage.

When Jon Irenicus's first ability resolves, the opponent will gain control of a creature and that creature will immediately gain “This creature can't be sacrificed” as part of the resolution of the ability. There is no window of opportunity for that player to sacrifice that creature before it gains the ability.

interactions.title: Donated liabilities come home if the holder leaves the game
interactions.ruling:
When a player leaves the game, every effect giving them control of something ends. A permanent you own that you gave away with Donate, Harmless Offering, Fateful Handoff or Blim comes back to you; Blim's ruling confirms this. That's dangerous for the liabilities:
- **Demonic Pact:** if the holder dies to something else before their upkeep, it comes back with only "You lose the game" left.
- **Archfiend of the Dross:** comes back with its remaining oil counters.
- **Immortal Coil:** comes back and triggers if your own graveyard is empty.
- **Greed's Gambit:** comes back with its end-step liabilities, and its leave liabilities if it later leaves.

Captive Audience and Xantcha are different: they entered under the other player's control, so they're exiled instead. Plan kill order so you aren't the next holder, or remove the returned card quickly.
interactions.short: Kill the holder some other way and Pact / Archfiend / Coil / Gambit return to you.

flag.note: In multiplayer, killing a Pact / Archfiend / Coil / Gambit holder some other way returns the liability to you (CR 800.4a). Sequence the kills or have removal ready.

oracle.quote: At the beginning of your upkeep, remove an oil counter from this creature. Then if it has no oil counters on it, you lose the game.

rulings.quote: The control-change effect of Blim's ability lasts indefinitely. It doesn't wear off during the cleanup step, and it doesn't expire if Blim leaves the battlefield. In a multiplayer game, it does expire if the current controller leaves the game.

In a multiplayer game, if Captive Audience’s owner leaves the game, Captive Audience leaves the game with them. If Captive Audience’s controller leaves the game, Captive Audience is exiled (assuming that player wasn’t also Captive Audience’s owner).

interactions.title: Greed's Gambit: the liabilities follow the controller, and they're at the end step, not upkeep
interactions.ruling: Greed's Gambit gives its controller three cards, 6 life and three Bats when it enters. After that, its end-step trigger and leave trigger affect whoever controls it then. Give it away and the recipient discards, loses 2 and sacrifices a creature each end step, plus discards three, loses 6 and sacrifices three when it leaves. The attestation calls these the "later upkeep" liabilities, but the Oracle trigger is at the beginning of your end step. The strategy is unaffected.

flag.note: Source attestation says Greed's Gambit's recurring liability is at upkeep; Oracle says end step.

oracle.quote: At the beginning of your end step, you discard a card, lose 2 life, and sacrifice a creature.
When this enchantment leaves the battlefield, you discard three cards, lose 6 life, and sacrifice three creatures.

interactions.title: Support pieces: Mana Vault, Withering Torment, Deflecting Swat
interactions.ruling: Mana Vault is just three colorless toward the five-mana commander; there's no Vault combo here. Withering Torment is instant-speed creature or enchantment removal and can kill a Pact or Audience you no longer want. You lose 2 only if it resolves. Deflecting Swat is free while you control a commander and protects without shroud.

oracle.quote: If you control a commander, you may cast this spell without paying its mana cost.

rulings.quote: If the target creature or enchantment is an illegal target as Withering Torment tries to resolve, it won't resolve and none of its effects will happen. You won't lose life.
